author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Practical Kind of Courage
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The trainee asked Danse why the workshop safety handbook had a section titled IDENTIFY UNTRUSTWORTHY PERSONNEL.

The question landed in the room like a dropped wrench.

Renn was an adult apprentice from a border settlement who had come to Brasswatch for a short training placement. They were learning to maintain water pumps and repair simple metal fittings. They had proved patient with measurements, careful with tools, and completely uninterested in the idea that a former Paladin's reputation should end a conversation.

Danse looked at the page.

"That section was copied from an older manual."

"Why is it still here?" Renn asked.

He didn't answer immediately.

I was at the next table checking the revised payment records. Ash was working in the adjoining room, where the private door now locked from the inside. They could hear the discussion, but nobody had asked them to participate.

Renn tapped the page.

"It says unfamiliar people should be reported until their origin is confirmed. That sounds like a reason to watch everyone who comes through the Threadways."

Danse rubbed a hand across his jaw.

"It was written for a military environment."

"Is the workshop a military environment?"

"No."

"Then why are we teaching it?"

I looked at him.

He met my eyes, then looked back at the trainee.

"You're right."

Renn blinked.

"I am?"

"Yes. That section doesn't belong in this handbook."

It could have ended there, with a simple correction and everyone returning to work.

But Danse was staring at the page with the expression of someone who had discovered an old voice speaking through his own handwriting.

"I used to believe those procedures were necessary," he said. "I enforced them."

Renn waited.

"That doesn't make them correct," Danse continued. "And it doesn't make the people affected by them responsible for making me feel better about changing."

I set down the ledger.

It wasn't a polished apology. It was better.

Renn looked at him.

"Then can we write a new rule?"

"Yes."

They pulled a blank sheet from the drawer.

The new section would concern actual safety behavior: handling hazardous materials, keeping exit routes clear, documenting threats without profiling visitors, asking consent before examining personal belongings, and protecting private information unless there was a specific, immediate danger.

It would not require anyone to disclose a homeworld, identity, or past allegiance merely to receive repair service.

I helped check the wording.

"How do we make sure people actually follow it?" Renn asked.

"Training," Danse said.

"And consequences," I added.

He nodded.

"Consequences."

By noon, we had revised three pages.

The work revealed other old assumptions. One instruction required the person in charge to approve every emergency exit. That made sense for a locked armory and no sense for a public workshop where people might need to leave during a fire.

Another said workers should ignore a task interruption until given permission to stop. That was how injuries happened.

Renn crossed it out.

Danse watched them.

"Are you angry?" he asked.

"At the old handbook? Yes."

"At me?"

Renn thought about it.

"A little. But mostly I want to know whether this place will be different."

Danse nodded.

"Then judge the changes we make."

I could see how hard it was for him not to ask for forgiveness, not to explain his old reasoning until it sounded noble. He let the discomfort stay.

That afternoon we tested the new emergency procedure.

Pip played the role of someone arriving with a box of loose fittings and no appointment. Edda tested the public entrance. Renn simulated a small electrical fault using a disconnected training board. Ash chose to observe from the private workroom with the door closed.

Danse did not order anyone to reveal where they came from.

He asked where help was needed.

When Renn reported the simulated fault, the group used the accessible exit and left the tools behind. The test wasn't perfect. Someone had to move a cart out of the way. The alarm cord was too high for one visitor. We wrote both problems down.

"Again tomorrow," Danse said.

Renn smiled.

"Good."

After the shift, I found Danse alone in the storage shed looking at the old handbook. He had separated the discarded pages from those still useful. The paper smelled of oil and dust.

"Will you burn it?" I asked.

He shook his head.

"I want to keep one copy as an example of what not to teach."

"With notes?"

"With notes."

I sat beside him.

"Does it feel strange?"

"Very."

He looked down at the title.

"There was a time when I thought courage meant obeying the right order despite fear. Later I thought it meant refusing an order that was wrong. Today I had to admit that I was still teaching part of the wrong order without noticing."

"That's a different kind of courage."

"Not an exciting one."

"Most useful courage isn't."

He smiled at that.

We watched the evening settle over Brasswatch Yard. Workers were closing the safe storage shed, and the hand pump was being checked one last time before the night rota began.

"Do you think Renn will come back tomorrow?" he asked.

"Probably. You paid them, listened, and let them correct you."

"That seems like a low standard."

"It's a beginning."

He took my hand.

"I want to build something people can trust."

"Then keep asking them what works."

He turned toward me.

"Do you trust me?"

The question was quiet enough that I almost missed it.

"I trust you to tell me the truth about what you're trying to change," I said. "And I trust myself to tell you when something still hurts. I don't need to pretend the past is harmless to love you now."

He looked at me for a long moment.

Then he lifted my hand to his lips.

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For not calling it finished."

I leaned close. He kissed me slowly, with none of the stiffness that had once made him hold every tender gesture like a military inspection. His hand rested gently against my cheek, and I smiled into the kiss.

"Come home," I whispered.

He nodded.

We left the old handbook on the table, marked for revision.

The following morning, Renn arrived with two new questions and a better drawing of the emergency exit.

Danse greeted them at the door.

"Good morning," he said. "What have I missed?"

Renn grinned.

"Plenty."

He held the door open.

"Then let's get to work."
